sec.title: Background
sec.p: For laying hens in the late stage of peak production, dysregulated liver lipids are one of the leading causes of declining egg production. Glucuronolactone (D-Glu) is used as a functional beverage additive in human food products and has been reported to play a role in lipid metabolism. However, its use with laying hens is rarely reported. This study integrated in vitro avian hepatocyte culture (LMH) models and in vivo laying hen trials to investigate the regulatory effects of D-Glu on hepatic lipid deposition.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: D-Glu significantly reduced intracellular lipid deposition in hepatocytes both in vivo and in vitro models, while also improving the production performance of laying hens. Liver lipidomic profiling revealed that D-Glu supplementation increased hepatic phospholipid abundance and reduced triglyceride (TG) accumulation, particularly by decreasing TG species enriched with polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA). This reduction in hepatic lipids is achieved by downregulating genes associated with fatty acid (FA) synthesis (FASN, ACSL, and PPAR-γ) and transport (FABP1 and CD36) pathways in the liver. Notably, D-Glu administration modulated the relative abundance of specific bacteria, particularly Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella, during hepatic lipid reduction mediation. Furthermore, D-Glu modified the composition of FA in the yolk, increasing the deposition of PUFA. Correlation analyses strongly supported the involvement of the enterohepatic axis in the lipid-lowering mechanism of D-Glu.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: D-Glu mediates lipid redistribution via the enterohepatic axis, effectively reducing hepatic lipid deposition while promoting the deposition of PUFA in egg yolk, ultimately alleviating the decline in production performance during the late peak laying period.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: As a kind of lipid metabolism disorder, fatty liver syndrome (FLS) is the most common noninfectious cause of mortality in laying backyard chickens throughout the world [1]. Notably, 74% of mortality in caged hens confirmed by necropsy was attributable to FLS [2]. This unresolved malady in laying hens (anecdotally termed "the silent killer") results in significant economic losses for caged egg producers through both acute and chronic manifestations [3]. During prolonged high-production laying cycles, excessive hepatic lipid deposition, along with injury, has been associated with FLS and causes substantial economic losses in the poultry industry [3]. Consequently, mitigating hepatic lipidosis during regular production cycles and reducing the "silent" adverse effects of lipid accumulation on the liver are critical for FLS prevention in the poultry industry. Among the various strategies for managing FLS, feed additives are considered one of the most efficient and convenient approaches, which can enhance intestinal and hepatic health, as well as overall productivity in laying hens. Probiotics, polysaccharides, and plant extracts can achieve this by improving redox balance, altering the gut microbiota, thereby modulating the hepatic lipidosis [4–6].

D-Glucuronolactone (D-Glu), a natural metabolite derived from glucose hydrolysis in the liver, is present in human connective tissues [7]. At physiological pH, D-Glu exists in equilibrium with its immediate precursor, glucuronic acid. D-Glu has been reported to promote detoxification of free hormones and other toxic chemicals in humans [8]. Thus, it has been used to support liver disease management for several years [9]. Detoxifying effects of D-Glu in hepatic cells and the central nervous system have been reported in animal models [10, 11]. Additionally, D-Glu has been shown to prevent muscular glycogen depletion by inhibiting substrate-mediated glycogenolysis [12]. Meanwhile, others have reported that D-Glu exerts beneficial effects by inhibiting amylase and β-glucosidase, thus increasing glucose consumption and glycogen synthesis [13]. To our knowledge, few studies have evaluated the effects of D-Glu on animals, especially the lipid-lowering effect. Given the limited reports, a preliminary evaluation was conducted to assess its impact on liver health in laying hens at various dosages. It was observed that D-Glu generally improved liver health, particularly by reducing total liver lipid content [14]. However, this effect needs to be further verified. Meanwhile, the underlying mechanism by which D-Glu reduces lipids in laying hens needs to be further elucidated.

Excessive accumulation of hepatic lipogenesis products, such as triglyceride (TG) and diglyceride (DG), is a key pathogenic feature of FLS, a condition projected to become a leading cause of advanced liver disease [15]. The hen's liver contributes to over 90% of de novo lipogenesis. Hence, the lipid classes deposited in the liver have various biological functions, including cellular signaling, energy metabolism, and regulatory roles in FLS [16, 17]. Dietary lipids are transported through the portal venous system to the liver following intestinal absorption. Once in the liver, these lipids are incorporated into lipoprotein particles, particularly yolk-targeted very low-density lipoprotein (VLDLy), which is specifically designed for yolk deposition [18]. These lipoproteins efficiently transport lipids to developing oocytes, where the lipids are integrated into the yolk matrix, providing essential components for embryonic development [19, 20]. As a result, the enterohepatic axis acts as a central regulatory pathway for the biosynthesis and distribution of yolk fatty acid (FA) during egg formation [21]. Studies have shown that some feed additives can influence hepatic lipid metabolism through the enterohepatic axis, thereby affecting the FA composition of egg yolk [22]. However, it remains unclear whether changes in hepatic lipid metabolism impact the composition of extrahepatic lipid in hens. These findings lead to the hypothesis that D-Glu may also affect lipid deposition in extrahepatic sites via the enterohepatic axis, such as abdominal fat and egg yolk. Furthermore, the effects of D-Glu on the intestinal microbiota and yolk FA composition in hens have not yet been documented.

This study aims to further investigate the effects of D-Glu on hepatic lipid metabolism and to explore the underlying mechanisms involved. We utilized both an in vitro model (LMH avian hepatocyte culture) and an in vivo model for this investigation. To test our hypotheses, we selected the control group and the most effective dose group from a preliminary study to analyze the impact of D-Glu through the enterohepatic axis. Lipidomics and microbiome analysis were included in this exploration. The findings of this study could provide a theoretical basis and research foundation for using D-Glu to alleviate FLS in laying hens.

sec.title: Cell culture, model-building and D-Glu intervention
sec.p: A hepatocellular carcinoma cell line (LMH cells) isolated from the liver of laying hens was purchased from North Carolina Souren Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (BNCC337930; Suzhou, Jiangsu, China) and cultured according to the provided instructions. The identity of LMH cells was confirmed by growth morphology observation and Short Tandem Repeat (STR) profiling. Furthermore, all cells were confirmed to be free of mycoplasma contamination using a mycoplasma detection kit before the trial commenced. Palmitic acid (PA), a well-known inducer of hepatic steatosis, was selected to induce fatty deposition in vitro [23]. Tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP) was employed as an exogenous inducer of lipid peroxidation [24]. LMH cells were exposed to different doses of PA or tBHP for 24 h. Cell viability was used to access the construction of the fatty deposition or lipid peroxidation model. The CCK-8 Cell Assay Kit (CA1210, Solarbio, Beijing, China) was used to detect cell viability. Based on cell viability experiments, an appropriate dosage of PA or tBHP were selected for subsequent experiments. Following pre-treatment with PA or tBHP, cells was treated with 1–400 μmol/L of D-Glu in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 12 h. After detecting cell viability, an appropriate dosage of D-Glu was chosen for subsequent experiments.

LMH cells were treated with PA and D-Glu using a 2 × 2 factorial design. An Oil Red O staining kit (G1262, Solarbio, Beijing, China) was used to stain lipid droplets in cultured LMH cells. The intracellular protein concentration and TG content in each group of cells were detected using commercial kits from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (A045-2-1 and A110-1-1; Nanjing, China).

LMH cells were treated with tBHP and D-Glu using a 2 × 2 factorial design. The levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were detected and monitored in each group of cells. ROS levels were assessed using a ROS detection kit (C2938, Invitrogen, USA) that measured the conversion of cell-permeable 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA) into the fluorescent molecule dichlorofluorescein (DCF) via an oxidative reaction. Readings were obtained using a microplate reader (Infinite M200 Pro, Tecan, Switzerland). The peak excitation and emission wavelengths of DCF fluorescence were 488 nm and 525 nm, respectively. The fluorescence in LMH cells was also observed under a microscope (DM 4000B, Leica, USA).

sec.title: Animals, experimental design and animal management
sec.p: Hy-Line brown laying hens, known for their high egg production, were selected at 42 weeks of age as a natural model susceptible to FLS, which is induced by the stress of long-term hepatic lipogenesis [25]. This age coincides with the late peak of the hens' laying period. A total of 256 Hy-Line brown hens were randomly divided into two groups, each consisting of eight replicates. The egg-laying rates were both high (over 95%) and comparable between the two groups prior to the trial. The hens were housed in individual step cages measuring 23 cm × 40 cm × 40 cm. Each experimental unit included 16 hens (one per cage), and they were collectively fed through a feed trough. The cages were placed in a ventilated room maintained at a temperature of 18–20 °C, with feeding occurring at regular intervals (08:00 and 15:00). The hens had ad libitum access to water from nipple drinkers and feed from troughs. Eggs were collected daily at 14:00. D-Glu supplementation was performed at a dosage calculated according to the recommendations of the European Food Safety Authority [26]. The required dosage of D-Glu was calculated as follows: (14 mg/kg body weight/d) × 2 kg body weight/(100 g feed intake) = 280 mg/kg diet. This amount was established as the highest level for hens in the preliminary trial. Following a comprehensive evaluation of performance and liver health outcomes, 280 mg/kg was determined to be the optimal level for this study.

After 1 week of adaptation, hens were given a basal (CON) or D-Glu-supplemented (280 mg/kg diet) diet for 12 weeks. D-Glu (purity ≥ 95%) was supplied by Howtian Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (Shandong province, China). The composition and nutritional levels of the basal diet are displayed in Table 1. sec.title: Collection of tissue samples
sec.p: At the end of the 12th week, one hen from each replicate was randomly selected and euthanized by cutting the jugular vein. Eggs were collected from each selected hen, and the yolks were stored at −80 °C for subsequent experiments. Abdominal fat was then removed from the hens and weighed to calculate the organ index (organ weight/body weight, g/g). The abdominal fat thickness was measured at three sites using vernier calipers, and the average was calculated. Measurements were taken from the left, center, and right locations, with the midpoints of the rectus abdominis being selected for the left and right measurements. Each hen's liver was photographed for clinical score grading [31]. Liver tissues were collected; most were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C, while the remaining tissues were sectioned after embedding in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound for Oil Red O staining and stored at −20 °C. Staining was performed as described in our previous study [30]. Additionally, the cecal contents from each hen were collected and stored at −80 °C for 16S analysis.

sec.title: Biochemical analysis
sec.p: The contents of TG (A110-1-1) and total cholesterol (TC; A111-1-1) in the egg yolk were measured using commercial assay kits purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (China).

sec.title: qRT‐PCR analysis
sec.p: The TRIzol (DP421, TianGen, Beijing, China) method was used to extract RNA from liver tissues. The relative mRNA expression levels were normalized to avian β-actin according to the 2−△△Ct method as described in a previous study [30]. Primer information is listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Untargeted liver lipidomic analysis with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
sec.p: Liver lipidomic analyses were performed using an ultra-high performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) system (UPLC, Agilent 1290, USA; MS, AB6600 SCIEX, USA). Duplicate samples underwent solvent addition in EP tubes followed by cryogenic homogenization, ultrasonic extraction in an ice bath, and incubation at −40 °C. Processed mixtures were centrifuged under refrigeration, with supernatants filtered through 0.22-μm organic membranes before −80 °C storage for LC–MS. Quality control samples were generated by pooling aliquots from all samples.

Chromatographic separation was used with a Phenomenex Kinetex C18 column (2.1 mm × 100 mm, 1.7 μm) maintained at 55 °C. The temperature of the autosampler was 8 °C. Gradient elution of analytes was carried out with acetonitrile:water = 60:40 (10 mmol/L ammonium formate) (A) and isopropanol:acetonitrile = 90:10 (10 mmol/L ammonium formate) (B) at a flow rate of 0.30 mL/min. The injection volume was 2 μL in positive mode and 2 μL in negative mode. An increasing linear gradient of solvent B (v/v) was used as follows: 0–1.5 min, 40% B; 1.5–10.5 min, 40%–85% B; 10.5–14 min, 85% B; 14–14.1 min, 85–100% B; 14.1–15 min, 100% B; 15–15.2 min, 100%–40% B; 15.2–18 min, 40% B.

The mass spectrometry parameters were used as follows: ion source gas 1 (GS1), 60 psi, ion source gas 2 (GS2), 60 psi, curtain gas (CUR), 30 psi, temperature, 600 °C; Ions pray voltage floating (ISVF), 5,000 V or 4,500 V in positive or negative modes, respectively; Delustering potential (DP) 100 V. Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) method was used for MS/MS acquisition. Each acquisition cycle consists of one rapid TOF MS survey scan (200 MS) followed by the consecutive acquisition of 11 product ion scans (50 MS each). For TOF MS survey scan, the mass range is from 200 to 2,000 Da, and collision energy (CE) is set as 10 V. For product ion scan, the mass ranges are from 100 to 2,000 Da, and CE is set as 45 ± 25 V. Dynamic background subtraction was applied. Dynamic exclusion was implemented to remove some unnecessary information in MS/MS spectra.

Raw data were annotated based on the Lipid Structure Database (LMSD; http://www.lipidmaps.org/) and assessed by orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA). Lipid species with a variable importance in projection (VIP) of > 1 and P-value of < 0.05 were identified as statistically significant.

sec.title: DNA extraction, 16S rRNA sequencing and bioinformatics analysis of cecal contents
sec.p: Genomic DNA was isolated from avian cecal homogenates employing a commercial extraction system (Omega Bio-Tek, USA) followed by cryopreservation at −20 °C. Microbial community profiling targeted the hypervariable V3–V4 regions of 16S rRNA genes through amplification with universal primers 515F/806R, referencing established methodologies. Dual-index paired-end sequencing conducted at Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) generated raw datasets, which underwent quality-controlled processing via Cutadapt (v1.9.1), with subsequent denoising and amplicon sequence variant (ASV) clustering performed using the UPARSE algorithm (v7.0.1001). Taxonomic assignment against the SILVA v132 reference database (https://www.arb-silva.de/) facilitated microbial classification.

To assess microbial heterogeneity, within-community (α-diversity) and inter-sample (β-diversity) metrics were computed, wherein α-diversity indices underwent Tukey's HSD post-hoc testing while β-diversity dissimilarities were subjected to permutational multivariate analysis of variance.

sec.title: Targeted metabolomic analysis of FA contents in egg yolk
sec.p: An appropriate amount (500 mg) of yolk sample was homogenized with glass beads in a chloroform–methanol solution (2:1, v/v). After centrifugation, the supernatant was collected and vortexed thoroughly with 1% sulfuric acid–methanol solution. Following esterification at 80 °C in a water bath, n-hexane was added. This supernatant was then treated with anhydrous sodium sulfate powder to remove residual water. Finally, methyl salicylate (500 mg/L) was added as an internal standard to the supernatant. The processed samples were vortexed before GC–MS analysis. Mixed standard stock solutions of 51 FA species were prepared to generate calibration curves.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The data were arranged using Excel. Gene data and lipid metabolite data were log10-transformed before statistical analysis if they did not follow a normal distribution. Differences between groups in vitro trial were examined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Duncan’s post hoc test, when the homogeneity of variance is not significant (P > 0.05). The differences between the two groups in vivo trial were analyzed by a t-test. The results were presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 8), and P < 0.05 indicated statistical significance. In all figures, * indicates P < 0.05.

The LION/web lipid ontology database was used to classify all the differential lipids using the Leiden community classification algorithm for the network analysis of lipid function enrichment [32]. Spearman correlation analysis was conducted on an online platform (https://www.omicstudio.cn) to identify the potential core metabolites or bacteria in hens.

sec.title: D-Glu ameliorates drug-induced lipid accumulation and oxidative damage in LMH cells
sec.p:
To evaluate the effects of D-Glu in LMH cells, a high-fat model was established by inducing lipid accumulation with PA. Concentrations of PA ranging from 400 to 800 μmol/L significantly decreased cell viability (Fig. S1A). Subsequently, the cells were treated with various concentrations of D-Glu (1–400 μmol/L) alongside 400 μmol/L PA. As illustrated in Fig. S1B, a concentration of 100 μmol/L D-Glu improved the viability of PA-treated cells. D-Glu treatment also significantly reduced TG content and the area of lipid droplets (P < 0.05; Fig. 1A, B). Representative photomicrographs of Oil Red O staining are presented in Fig. 1C. The red arrow indicates an intracellular lipid droplet.Fig. 1
D-Glu ameliorates drug-induced lipid accumulation and oxidative damage in LMH cells. LMH cells were left untreated or pre-treated with D-Glu before a PA or tBHP challenge. A TG levels. B Area of lipid droplets determined based on Oil Red O staining. C Representative images showing Oil Red O staining in LMH cells. Scale bar: 20 μm. The red arrow indicates an intracellular lipid droplet. D ROS levels. E Representative images of ROS levels obtained based on DCF fluorescence. Scale bar: 10 μm. *P < 0.05

To model oxidative damage in LMH cells, a lipid peroxidation model was created using tBHP. Concentrations of tBHP from 400 to 800 μmol/L significantly decreased cell viability (Fig. S1C). Following tBHP treatment, the cells were incubated with graded concentrations of D-Glu (1–400 μmol/L). D-Glu at 100 μmol/L enhanced the viability of tBHP-treated cells (Fig. S1D). Furthermore, D-Glu treatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, as evidenced by the intensity of DCF fluorescence (P < 0.05; Fig. 1D). Representative fluorescence photomicrographs of ROS are shown in Fig. 1E.

sec.title: D-Glu improves laying performance and ameliorates lipid deposition in laying hens
sec.p:
The experimental design is illustrated in Fig. 2A. Figure 2B presents the run chart of laying performance across different weeks. The addition of D-Glu to the diet significantly improved both the egg laying rate and egg mass throughout the study period. This beneficial effect was particularly pronounced in the latter part of the experiment. No significant differences were observed in average egg weight or average daily feed intake.Fig. 2

Hens received either a basal diet or a basal diet supplemented with D-Glu for 12 weeks (n = 8 per group). B Run chart of laying performance, including the laying rate, egg mass, average egg weight, and feed/egg ratio of hens throughout the trial. C Representative photographs of the liver in the control group and D-Glu treatment group. D Representative photographs of Oil Red O stained liver tissues from the control and D-Glu treatment groups. Scale bar: 75 μm. E Effects of D-Glu on the FLS score and lipid droplets area of liver. F Effects of D-Glu on the percentage and width of abdominal fat. Representative images of hen livers from both the control and D-Glu treatment groups are shown in Fig. 2C. The livers from the control hens exhibited a yellow discoloration, while the livers from the D-Glu-treated hens displayed a normal reddish coloration. Representative liver sections stained with Oil Red O are presented in Fig. 2D, showing significantly fewer lipid droplets in the D-Glu-treated hens compared to the controls (P < 0.001; Fig. 2E). D-Glu supplementation also significantly reduced fatty liver scores (P = 0.049; Fig. 2E). Additionally, D-Glu significantly decreased the width of the abdominal fat pad (P = 0.002) without affecting the percentage of abdominal fat (P > 0.10; Fig. 2F). There were no significant changes in TG or total cholesterol (TC) deposition in the yolk due to D-Glu supplementation (P = 0.254 and P = 0.720, respectively; Fig. 2G).

sec.title: Lipidomic analysis reveals that D-Glu alters the hepatic lipid profile in laying hens
sec.p: Lipidomic analysis indicates that D-Glu affects the hepatic lipid profile in laying hens. The quality of the data obtained was evaluated based on the reproducibility of quality control (QC) samples. Important parameters included the coincidence of QC samples (see Fig. S2) and the relative standard deviation (RSD; see Fig. S3). In the principal component analysis (PCA) plots, we observed tight clustering of the QC samples. Additionally, peaks with an RSD of less than 30% accounted for 84.5% of the total peaks detected in the QC samples. These results suggest that the lipidomics data are both stable and reliable.

OPLS-DA was conducted to identify the overall metabolic differences between the groups and to evaluate the variation within samples from the same group. The results showed a clear distinction between the liver samples from the D-Glu group and those from the control group, highlighting significant differences in hepatic lipid profiles. The OPLS-DA model used to compare the control and D-Glu groups produced the following parameters: R2X = 0.60, R2Y = 0.91, and Q2 = 0.61. In this context, R2 reflects the model's explanatory power, while Q2 indicates its predictive capability. The OPLS-DA score plot (Fig. 3 A, B) clearly illustrated the separation of the D-Glu treatment group from the control group.Fig. 3
Lipidomic analysis reveals that D-Glu alters the hepatic lipid profile in laying hens. A OPLS-DA score plot of the control group and the D-Glu group; R2X = 0.641, R2Y = 0.996, and Q2 = 0.602. B Verification of the OPLS-DA model based on permutation test; R2 = 0.99, Q2 = 0.02. C Volcano plot showing differential lipid metabolites between the control group and the D-Glu group. D Heat maps generated using non-targeted lipidomics showing the levels of differential lipid metabolites. E Heat maps generated from (D) showing the levels of differential lipid classes. F LION enrichment of differential lipid metabolites

A total of 1,042 lipid molecules belonging to 16 different lipid classes were identified (Table S2). The peak intensities of these lipid molecules were compared between the control and D-Glu groups by analyzing their relative values using the log2 fold change (FC) and a significance threshold of P < 0.05 in the volcano plot (Fig. 3C). Ultimately, 87 differential lipid molecules were identified between the two groups. Of these, 29 lipids were upregulated in the D-Glu group compared to the control group, while 58 lipids were downregulated. The quantitative results and clustering heat maps for these 87 differential metabolites are displayed in Fig. 3D. Notably, some lipid molecules within the same class exhibited opposing trends in expression. To further investigate the lipid alterations induced by D-Glu, a cluster analysis based on lipid classes was conducted, as illustrated in Fig. 3E. Consistent with the results of the biochemical analysis, the lipidomics analysis revealed that D-Glu significantly decreased the DG and TG content in the liver. Additional analysis of the specific DG and TG species is presented later. The functional enrichment analysis of the significantly different lipids is shown in Fig. 3F. The differential lipids exhibited the most significant enrichment in the glycerol-phosphoethanolamine (GP02) pathway, the mitochondrial metabolism pathway, the metabolism of FA with carbon chain lengths of 22 to 24, and the pathway related to average bilayer thickness. Additionally, pathways related to cell membrane components, glycerophospholipid (GP) metabolism, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) metabolism demonstrated the highest levels of enrichment.

sec.title: The types and structure of FA attached to the glycerol backbone of TG or DG mediate the modulatory effect of D-Glu on the liver
sec.p:
To clarify the structural basis for reduced lipid deposition, we conducted a detailed examination of the differential lipids, focusing on their carbon chain lengths and saturation levels. These lipids were categorized according to their lipid classification, and specific calculations were performed to determine the number of carbon atoms and the degree of saturation (see Fig. 4A). Our structure-based analysis revealed a significantly decreased abundance of long-chain FA (i.e., C35–45) and polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA; with double-bond content between 3–6) in DG species treated with D-Glu, as indicated by the symbol and red color (P < 0.05). In the TG species, we observed a lower abundance of PUFA (with double-bond content between 3–10) and long-chain FA (C48–56) in the D-Glu treatment group (P < 0.05). Conversely, the abundance of saturated fatty acid (SFA) and unsaturated fatty acid (UFA) (with double-bond content between 0–3) significantly increased in the TG deposited in the liver (P < 0.05). Similar results were observed for the FA deposited in phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) classes (P < 0.05). These findings demonstrate that D-Glu reduces the overall incorporation of PUFA into various hepatic lipid classes, including DG, TG, PC, and PE.Fig. 4

Furthermore, we deeply analyzed the alterations of detailed species in TG and DG induced by D-Glu (Fig. 4B, C). Overall, the total amount of TG in the D-Glu treatment group was 5% lower than that in the control group, according to the lipidomic analysis data (P < 0.05). Among the TG species, the following contributed significantly to this reduction: TG (18:2–18:2–18:2), (18:1–18:2–16:0), (22:5–18:2–18:2), (17:0–18:2–18:2), (18:1–18:2–16:1), and (18:1–18:1–18:3). In the DG species, the most notable reductions were observed in DG (18:2–18:1), (18:2–18:2), (18:3–16:1), (18:2–17:1), and (18:2–20:1). These findings indicate that D-Glu significantly decreased the accumulation of FA with 18 carbons in the glycerol backbone, particularly C18:1 (oleic acid) and C18:2 (linoleic acid).

sec.title: D-Glu modulates lipid metabolism-related genes in hen’s liver
sec.p:
To gain a better understanding of how D-Glu alleviates FLS, we examined the expression of genes involved in FA synthesis, transport, β-oxidation, and lipid hydrolysis in the livers of laying hens (Fig. 5). Our analysis of gene expression in the FA synthesis pathway revealed that D-Glu supplementation significantly reduced the expression levels of FASN, ACSL, and PPAR-γ (P < 0.05). In contrast, it significantly increased the expression level of SREBP1C (P < 0.05; Fig. 5A). Regarding FA transport, D-Glu also significantly reduced the expression levels of CD36 and FABP1 (P < 0.05; Fig. 5B). Among the genes associated with TG hydrolysis, D-Glu showed a tendency to increase the expression of HSL (P = 0.056; Fig. 5C). However, D-Glu did not have a significant effect on the genes related to FA β-oxidation, as well as those related to ATGL and TC metabolism (P > 0.05).Fig. 5

sec.title: Microbiome analysis reveals that D-Glu alters the gut microbiota profile in laying hens
sec.p:
Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) of metagenomic sequencing data revealed distinct clustering between laying hens supplemented with D-Glu and control hens (Adonis test, P = 0.042; Fig. 6A). Alpha diversity indices are presented in Fig. 6B. No significant differences in Chao1 or Simpson index values were observed between groups (P > 0.05), indicating that D-Glu supplementation did not significantly alter cecal microbiota diversity. Based on PCoA results, relative cecal bacterial abundance was calculated at the phylum level (Fig. 6C). The dominant phyla (relative abundance > 2%) identified in the gut microbiota were Firmicutes and Bacteroidota, with Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and other minor phyla also present. In control hens, the relative abundances of Firmicutes and Bacteroidota were 45.2% and 44.12%, respectively. D-Glu supplementation significantly decreased the relative abundance of Firmicutes to 42.84% (P < 0.05) and significantly increased the relative abundance of Bacteroidota to 48.90% (P < 0.05). Consequently, the Firmicutes to Bacteroidota (F/B) ratio was significantly reduced (P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in the relative abundances of the remaining phyla (P > 0.05).Fig. 6
Microbiome analysis reveals that D-Glu alters the gut microbiota profile in laying hens. A PCoA and adonis test based on the Bray–Curtis distance of gut microbial functions among laying hens with and without dietary D-Glu. B Differences in the Shannon and Chao1 indices of α-diversity. C Column diagram of species relative abundance of top 10 at phylum level. D Variations in the relative abundance of different bacteria species in genus. E LEfSe analysis of differential species for biomarkers on microbiota structure in D-Glu groups. F Evolutionary branching diagram of 2 groups

To identify gut microbial genera potentially involved in the D-Glu-mediated lipid-lowering process, genera making substantial contributions to community differences and those exhibiting significant differences in relative abundance between groups were screened (Fig. 6D). Compared to the control group, the relative abundances of Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella were significantly increased (P < 0.05). The relative abundances of Ligilactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Fusobacterium showed a decreasing trend (P < 0.10).

LEfSe analysis further demonstrated that D-Glu increased the relative abundances of Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella, etc. (Fig. 6E). To further investigate the phylogenetic relationships among taxa at the genus level, representative sequences for the top 100 genera were obtained through multiple sequence alignment and are displayed in Fig. 6F. The phylogenetic tree constructed from these representative genus-level sequences is presented; branch and fan sector colors denote their corresponding phyla. Stacked bar charts on the outer ring of the fan chart illustrate the abundance distribution of each genus across different samples. Collectively, integrating the LEfSe results, the phylogenetic tree, and the significantly differential microbes identified, it is evident that Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella are implicated in the lipid lowering effects mediated by D-Glu.

sec.title: D-Glu alters egg yolk FA composition in laying hens
sec.p:
Given that gut microbiota modulates hepatic lipid metabolism, we examined whether D-Glu-induced microbial shifts influence yolk FA composition. Egg yolk FA composition is shown in Fig. 7. The relative proportion of SFA and UFA in total FA are shown in Fig. 7A and C, while the absolute contents of SFA and UFA detected in egg yolk are presented in Fig. 7B and D. D-Glu supplementation significantly increased the UFA content in yolk (P = 0.008; Fig. 7A, B), while showed no effects on SFA content (P > 0.05; Fig. 7C and D). This increase in total UFA was primarily driven by elevated PUFA content (Fig. 7E), whereas monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) levels remained similar between groups (Fig. 7F).Fig. 7
D-Glu alters egg yolk FA composition in laying hens. A–B Differences in the relative abundance (A) and content (B) of SFA in egg yolk. C–D Differences in the relative abundance (C) and content (D) of UFA in egg yolk. E–F Differences in the relative abundance of MUFA (E) and PUFA (F) in egg yolk. G–I Differences in the detailed contents of SFA (G), MUFA (H), and PUFA (I) of the egg yolk

Specifically, D-Glu significantly increased concentrations of some SFA: pentadecanoic acid (C15:0), heptadecanoic acid (C17:0), and stearic acid (C18:0) (P < 0.05; Fig. 7G). Among MUFA, levels of heptadecenoic acid (C17:1), oleic acid (C18:1n9c), and eicosenoic acid (C20:1) were significantly elevated in the D-Glu group compared to controls (P < 0.05; Fig. 7H). Multiple PUFA, including linoleic acid (C18:2n6), sciadonic acid (C20:3n6), arachidonic acid (C20:4n6), and docosapentaenoic acid (C22:5n6), exhibited significantly higher concentrations in the D-Glu group versus controls (P < 0.05; Fig. 7I). Additionally, γ-linolenic acid (C18:3n6) and docosatetraenoic acid (C22:4) tended to increase in the D-Glu group (P < 0.10; Fig. 7H). These findings indicate that D-Glu can enhance the nutritional richness of egg yolk through increased deposition of PUFA.

sec.title: Correlation analysis
sec.p:
We then analyzed the relationship between different lipid classes and lipid phenotypes in laying hens. The heat map analysis showed positive correlations between indicators of hepatic fat (e.g., TG content, liver weight, liver index, fatty liver score, and abdominal fat width) and neutral lipids (TG and DG) that assessed in lipidomic analysis. Conversely, there were negative correlations with phospholipid content (Fig. 8A).Fig. 8
Correlation analysis. A Correlation analysis between lipid concentration and laying performance, hepatic lipid-related indexes, lipid deposition outside the liver, and the expression of FA metabolism-related genes in hens. B Correlation analysis between down-regulated lipid species in liver, up-regulated FA in yolk and differential microbial taxa in cecum

To investigate the potential regulatory relationships between gut microbes and metabolites, correlation analyses were performed among downregulated hepatic lipid species, upregulated yolk FA, and differential cecal microbial taxa. The results are presented in Fig. 8B. The upper-right section displays a correlation heat map between lipid metabolites and FA, while the lower-left section represents associations between microbiota and metabolites. Metabolite-metabolite correlations are color-coded, with blue indicating negative correlations and red indicating positive correlations. The associations between microbiota and metabolites are illustrated by connecting lines, where the thickness of the line denotes the strength of the correlation, and the color of the line indicates the statistical significance level (P-value). Significant negative correlations were found between the upregulated yolk FA species and the downregulated hepatic lipids (P < 0.05). Specifically, Bacteroides was significantly associated with the hepatic levels of TG (18:1–18:1–18:3) and TG (18:2–18:2–18:2). In addition, Angelakisella showed significant correlations with multiple lipid species that were reduced in the liver, including DG (18:3–16:1), DG (20:1–18:2), TG (18:1–18:1–18:2), and TG (18:1–18–18:2) (P < 0.05). All these lipid species were significantly reduced in the livers of hens following D-Glu supplementation. Furthermore, the abundance of CHKCI001 and Angelakisella was correlated with the PUFA content in egg yolk, such as C20:4N6 and C22:5N5.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: FLS, caused by abnormal lipid metabolism in the liver, results in significant economic losses in the commercial production of laying hens. D-Glu, a common ingredient in many energy drinks, has been reported to have hepatoprotective and lipid-lowering effects [9, 33]. However, research on its impact on hepatic lipid deposition in hens has been limited. In this study, we found that the dietary administration of D-Glu effectively reduces lipid deposition both in vitro and in vivo. This effect is associated with a remodeling of the hepatic lipid profile in the livers of hens. Additionally, the gut microbiota plays a positive role in this process. The effect of D-Glu on hepatic lipids is also reflected in the FA composition of the egg yolk.

In recent years, there have been few reports on the use of D-Glu for modulating lipid metabolism, especially in poultry species. A previous study highlighted the detoxification and antioxidant effects of D-Glu on poultry embryonic cells under toxic conditions [10]. To date, studies investigating the lipid-lowering effect of D-Glu have often used a combination of D-Glu or glucuronic acid along with other components [12, 34]. Notably, D-Glu supplementation alone has been shown to positively impact both performance and lipid metabolism in laying hens. The current findings indicate that D-Glu has beneficial lipid-reducing effects on both LMH cells and the liver of laying hens, ultimately leading to improved production performance. Lipid accumulation is not only characteristic of FLS but also contributes to lipid peroxidation and liver damage [35]. Results from LMH cells revealed that D-Glu effectively reverses oxidative stress and hepatic steatosis caused by lipid accumulation. Additionally, in vivo results indicated that the reduction of hepatic lipid deposition in laying hens coincided with improved production performance during the final phase of the trial. This suggests a positive correlation between liver health and laying performance in hens, which aligns with previous studies on FLS [36, 37].

Hens' livers are particularly susceptible to lipid deposition due to the high demands of egg-laying. This condition resembles the hallmark of FLS, resulting in a significant accumulation of lipids in hepatocytes [38, 39]. To better understand lipid metabolism, a common technique used is the assessment of FA flux. This process involves profiling non-esterified and esterified FA into various lipid classes, such as glycerolipids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, and cholesterol esters [40]. Therefore, the hepatic lipid profile may play a crucial role in analyzing disorders of lipid metabolism in laying hens. In the present study, the lipidomic profile indicated that D-Glu treatment increased the proportion of phospholipids while reducing the amount of neutral lipids in laying hens. Neutral glycerolipids mainly consist of TG, DG, and monoglycerides. Zhang et al. [41] reported that phospholipids dramatically decrease hepatic lipid accumulation in rat models of FLS induced by a high-fat diet. These findings suggest that elevated levels of hepatic phospholipids are generally associated with a decrease in neutral lipid content, reflecting a dynamically balanced state of intrahepatic lipid allocation. In the present study, the most enriched lipids in the D-Glu treatment group were found to be concentrated in metabolic pathways associated with GP, ER, and mitochondrial metabolism. It has been reported that both mitochondrial and ER metabolism play a role in the reconfiguration of lipids, suggesting that D-Glu treatment promotes the shift of hepatic lipids towards energy expenditure, thereby reducing their accumulation as TG [42]. Additionally, there was an increase in the levels of glycerophospholipid and ethanolamine derivatives. As essential components of cell membranes, the elevated levels of these lipids in the profile indicate that the liver is directing more lipids towards the creation of molecular and cellular bioenergetics in the D-Glu treatment group [43, 44]. It is hypothesized that D-Glu redirects energy and lipid flow towards bioenergetic processes rather than allowing for hepatic accumulation, facilitating the use of lipids as structural components of membranes during hepatocyte regeneration [45]. Similar hepatic lipidomic profile has been reported in previous studies, where a decrease in TG synthesis was accompanied by an increase in GP levels in human [46]. These results highlight a strong relationship between the types of lipids accumulated in the liver and their metabolic pathways, which are significantly influenced by D-Glu in laying hens.

Hepatic lipid structures were analyzed, with a specific focus on FA that were deposited in lipid molecules. Notably, D-Glu treatment significantly reduced the number of double bonds in the FA present in lipid classes, particularly in DG and TG. Previous studies have also observed an increased content of FA with fewer double bonds in lipids, suggesting that a higher liver fat content is associated with elevated levels of TG containing SFA or MUFA, as well as a decrease in PUFA-containing phospholipids and ether lipids [47]. Besides, the distribution and spatial specificity of FA on the glycerol backbone significantly influence the metabolism of lipid molecules, including their absorption and utilization [48]. UFA in TG species can be unstable and are prone to oxidation and degradation, which provides energy for cellular processes [49]. Additionally, lipids with a higher number of double bonds are more readily released into circulation for transport to peripheral tissues [50]. This may help explain the lipid-lowering effect of D-Glu on abdominal fat. These findings suggest that D-Glu alters the composition of FA deposited in lipids, thereby modifying lipid metabolic pathways and reducing the accumulation of hepatic lipids. Meanwhile, recent reports suggest that FA with increased double bonds raise the risk of peroxidation, which can be harmful to human health [51, 52]. ER stress has been linked to elevated levels of saturated TG precursors, impaired lipid formation, and increased order of the ER membrane [53]. Povero et al. [54] also indicated that the incorporation of PUFAs into membrane phospholipids, along with the delivery of SFAs to ceramide synthesis under hypoxic conditions, may worsen lipid peroxidation and apoptosis. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that D-glucose treatment mitigates hepatic ER and oxidative stress in hens, aligning with the results of our functional enrichment analysis. Additionally, the FA profiles in DG and TG showed that D-Glu significantly reduced the deposition of C18 FA, particularly linoleic (C18:2) and oleic (C18:1) acids. This reduction appears to correlate with the effects of dietary PUFA supplementation [55]. C18 FA are prevalent in livers affected by FLS in humans, rats, and hens [56, 57]. D-Glucose has been identified as playing a critical role in the metabolism and clearance of various endogenous and exogenous compounds, including FA [58]. Given the lack of significant effects on FA overall, we hypothesize that D-Glu selectively interacts with C18 FA and promotes their excretion through urine and feces, a process stimulated by UDP-glycosyltransferase. Therefore, our findings suggest that D-glucose may alter the types and locations of FA within TG molecules, with variations in FA species depending on carbon chain length and degree of saturation.

Hepatic steatosis is a central aspect of FLS and primarily results from an imbalance between the production and secretion of TG in the liver [59]. This condition occurs when the liver's production of TG, through processes like de novo lipogenesis and the uptake of FA from the bloodstream, exceeds its ability to oxidize FA and release TG via VLDL [60]. D-Glu has been observed to inhibit FA synthesis and transport by downregulating the expression of several key hepatic genes, including FASN, ACSL, CD36, FABP1, PPAR-γ, and HSL. This downregulation helps reduce adiposity in laying hens. Among these genes, FASN, ACSL, and PPAR-γ are considered core regulators of de novo FA synthesis [38]. The uptake of FA for TG synthesis is largely mediated by FATP and CD36 [61]. HSL is an important enzyme that facilitates the hydrolysis of TG to release free FA and glycerol in adipocytes. Inhibiting lipolysis through HSL inhibition may help prevent the accumulation of free FA [62]. These findings suggest that D-Glu treatment reduces both the synthesis and uptake of FA from the circulation while increasing the lipolysis of intrahepatic TG. This process may result in more FA being secreted through VLDL. However, both our lipidomic and mRNA analyses indicate that D-Glu has a limited impact on cholesterol metabolism.

An increasing number of studies clearly demonstrate that various mechanisms mediate the interactions between the gut—along with its microbial communities—and the liver [63]. In the present study, the supplementation of D-Glu significantly altered the composition of gut microbiota. This was characterized by an increase in the abundance of Firmicutes and a decrease in the abundance of Bacteroidetes at the phylum level. These findings resulted in a decrease in the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio. It is well established that an increased proportion of Firmicutes is associated with conditions such as obesity, FLS, and type 2 diabetes mellitus [64]. Elevated feed-to-body (F/B) ratios are associated with obesity and metabolic disorders, potentially due to increased caloric extraction from food, fat accumulation, lipogenesis, and impaired insulin sensitivity [65]. These findings suggest that the gut microbiota of long-term high-yield laying hens closely resembles that linked to lipid metabolism disorders. However, treatment with D-Glu gradually shifts the gut microbial composition of these hens toward a healthier state. Meanwhile, D-Glu administration also increases the relative abundances of specific genera, including Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella, which have been reported to mitigate FLS. Bacteroides, in particular, has been shown to improve FLS by promoting the proliferation of Akkermansia, restoring intestinal barrier integrity, and reducing inflammation [66]. Yang et al. [67] reported a negative correlation between the abundance of CHKCI001 and FLS biomarkers, suggesting that this taxon may mitigate the development of FLS. Based on these findings, along with results from LEfSe and correlation analyses, it appears that Angelakisella plays a significant role in the lipid-lowering process mediated by D-Glu. Notably, the content of Angelakisella was significantly correlated with FA in both liver and yolk. Additionally, studies in mice have shown a positive correlation between Angelakisella content and lipocalin-2 levels, while a negative correlation was observed with fecal short-chain FA, indicating its involvement in intestinal FA metabolism [68]. These findings suggest that D-Glu modulates gut microbiota abundance and influences the metabolism and deposition of FA through the enterohepatic axis.

The role of dietary D-Glu extends beyond simply reducing risks associated with hepatic lipid dysregulation; it also modulates the FA profiles in egg yolks by influencing liver lipid metabolism pathways in laying hens. The fats found in yolks are generated in the liver and transported through the bloodstream as TG-rich VLDL for deposition into the yolk [69]. The findings of this study show that dietary D-Glu supplementation significantly increases the UFA content in egg yolks, particularly enhancing the levels of omega-6 PUFA such as linoleic acid, linolenic acid, and arachidonic acid. Similar effects have been observed in studies involving N-carbamoylglutamate and mulberry branch fiber, where modulation of hepatic lipid metabolism led to an increase in nutritionally beneficial PUFA levels in yolks [22, 70]. Comparable effects have also been noted with L-arginine and glutamic acid on FA profiles in porcine muscle tissue [71]. Furthermore, there is a significant negative correlation between reduced hepatic lipids and increased yolk FA in hens. This suggests that the deposition of PUFA in tissues outside the liver is part of the process of hepatic lipid efflux, demonstrated by a reduction in liver lipid accumulation. These results highlight the importance of hepatic lipid metabolism in determining the deposition of extrahepatic lipids, particularly in yolk FA.

Finally, research has investigated the potential links between variations in gut microbiota and the lipid profiles of both the liver and yolk in laying hens. Correlation analyses revealed significant associations between hepatic lipidomic profiles and both intrahepatic and ectopic lipid deposition patterns. These findings support the hypothesis that PUFA within the liver are transported to extrahepatic tissues for deposition, which may contribute to lipid reduction. However, this proposed mechanism requires further verification. Additionally, specific gut bacteria, including Bacteroides, CHKCI001, and Angelakisella, play significant roles in this lipid repartitioning process. The correlation analysis suggests that CHKCI001 may be involved in the metabolism of FA deposited in the yolk, while Bacteroides seems to play a more prominent role in hepatic lipid metabolism. Notably, Angelakisella may be involved in both metabolic processes. These findings further underscore the importance of the enterohepatic axis in regulating lipid metabolism influenced by D-Glu.

Collectively, this study highlights the beneficial effects of D-Glu on the progression of FLS in hens, particularly from a lipid-lowering perspective. However, the specific mechanisms by which D-Glu alters the deposition of C18 FA in lipid molecules remain unclear. Importantly, laying hens are increasingly recognized as a valuable model for studying FLS and hepatic steatosis [36, 72]. This research offers a new perspective on preventing FLS in laying hens and suggests potential therapeutic applications for D-Glu.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that dietary D-Glu supplementation effectively reduced hepatic lipid deposition and improved laying performance in laying hens by remodeling hepatic lipid dynamics and downregulating key genes involved in FA metabolism. Moreover, D-Glu enriched beneficial gut microbiota and elevated PUFA in yolk. Collectively, D-Glu may mediate lipid redistribution in hens via the enterohepatic axis. These findings provide novel insights into the regulatory role of D-Glu as a promising nutritional strategy for preventing FLS and extending the laying cycle in hens.
